questions: Did these movements begin suddenly, over hours or a few days?
Did they begin after starting, stopping, or changing a medication?
Have you recently taken metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, promethazine, or another medication for nausea?
Have you recently taken an antipsychotic medication?
Have you recently taken an antidepressant, stimulant, anticonvulsant, steroid, or recreational drug?
Are the movements present when you are completely relaxed?
Can you voluntarily stop the movements for several seconds?
Do you feel an inner urge or tension before making the movements?
Do you feel relief after making the movements?
Do the movements lessen when you are distracted or concentrating on another task?
Do the movements disappear while you are asleep?
Have the movements been getting progressively worse?
Do the movements involve your face, mouth, or tongue?
Do the movements involve your legs or trunk?
Have you had episodes of staring, unresponsiveness, or loss of awareness?
Have you had a seizure or convulsion?
Have you had new weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, or trouble seeing?
Have you had confusion, memory problems, or a major change in your behavior?
Have you recently had severe anxiety, depression, hallucinations, or unusual beliefs?
Have you had fever or a recent infection?
Could you be pregnant or have you recently given birth?
Have you had unexplained weight loss, racing heartbeat, sweating, or heat intolerance?
Have you had jaundice or other liver problems?
Have you ever been diagnosed with Wilson disease or abnormal copper levels?
Has anyone in your family had similar involuntary movements?
Has anyone in your family had Huntington disease?
Have you ever had similar movements before?
Do you have a history of thyroid disease, autoimmune disease, or rheumatic disease?
Have you recently used cocaine, amphetamines, or other stimulants?
Have you recently stopped drinking alcohol or taking a sedative medication?
orders: Full bedside neurological examination, including strength, sensation, reflexes, coordination, eye movements, gait, and assessment for chorea, dystonia, rigidity, and cerebellar signs
Urgent MRI brain with and without gadolinium, including diffusion-weighted and susceptibility-weighted sequences
Complete blood count, electrolytes, renal function, liver enzymes, glucose, calcium, magnesium, and phosphate
C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and blood cultures
Lumbar puncture for opening pressure, cerebrospinal-fluid cell count and differential, protein, glucose, Gram stain, bacterial culture, viral PCR, and oligoclonal bands
Serum and cerebrospinal-fluid autoimmune encephalitis antibody panels, including NMDA-receptor, LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-B, AMPA, and DPPX antibodies
Serum antistreptolysin-O and anti-DNase B titers
Serum ANA, anti-dsDNA, ENA panel, complement levels, antiphospholipid antibodies, and ANCA
Thyroid-stimulating hormone, free thyroxine, thyroid antibodies, ceruloplasmin, and serum copper
HIV antigen/antibody, syphilis serology, and respiratory viral PCR testing
CT angiography of the head and neck if the focal neurological symptoms are acute or fluctuating
served: deep tendon reflexes and plantar responses
CSF oligoclonal bands and IgG index
results: 1. Full bedside neurological examination, including strength, sensation, reflexes, coordination, eye movements, gait, and assessment for chorea, dystonia, rigidity, and cerebellar signs
deep tendon reflexes and plantar responses: normal
coordination examination (limb and truncal): mild limb and truncal ataxia
2. Urgent MRI brain with and without gadolinium, including diffusion-weighted and susceptibility-weighted sequences
brain MRI: no cerebellar atrophy, no focal lesion
3. Complete blood count, electrolytes, renal function, liver enzymes, glucose, calcium, magnesium, and phosphate
serum electrolytes, urea and creatinine: normal
serum calcium, magnesium and phosphate: normal
4. C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and blood cultures
5. Lumbar puncture for opening pressure, cerebrospinal-fluid cell count and differential, protein, glucose, Gram stain, bacterial culture, viral PCR, and oligoclonal bands
lumbar puncture / CSF: normal cells, protein and glucose; no oligoclonal bands
CSF cell count and differential: normal
CSF oligoclonal bands and IgG index: normal
CSF culture and viral PCR: normal
6. Serum and cerebrospinal-fluid autoimmune encephalitis antibody panels, including NMDA-receptor, LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-B, AMPA, and DPPX antibodies
7. Serum antistreptolysin-O and anti-DNase B titers
8. Serum ANA, anti-dsDNA, ENA panel, complement levels, antiphospholipid antibodies, and ANCA
9. Thyroid-stimulating hormone, free thyroxine, thyroid antibodies, ceruloplasmin, and serum copper
copper / caeruloplasmin: normal - excludes Wilson disease
10. HIV antigen/antibody, syphilis serology, and respiratory viral PCR testing
EEG: no abnormality, and no EEG-EMG correlation on video-EEG - the myoclonus is subcortical
12. CT angiography of the head and neck if the focal neurological symptoms are acute or fluctuating

DIAGNOSIS: Post-COVID-19 subcortical myoclonus–ataxia syndrome (post-infectious COVID-19–associated myoclonus with cerebellar ataxia)

ALTERNATIVE: Functional movement disorder with functional gait ataxia

ALTERNATIVE: Post-streptococcal myoclonus–ataxia syndrome (Sydenham-spectrum disorder)
